steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Primary processing converts raw food materials into basic ingredients: milling wheat into flour, pasteurising milk, refining sugar cane, and slaughtering and butchering animals.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Secondary processing converts primary-processed ingredients into more complex products: making flour into bread, milk into cheese, flour and sugar into biscuits, potatoes into crisps.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Food additives are substances added to food for a specific purpose: preservatives (extend shelf life), colourants (improve appearance), flavourings (enhance taste), emulsifiers (mix oil and water), stabilisers (maintain texture).

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Additives are given E numbers when approved for use in the EU; some consumers prefer additive-free foods due to health concerns (e.g. hyperactivity linked to some colourants).

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: What is the difference between primary and secondary food processing? | Q: Name four types of food additive and their purpose. | Q: What is food fortification and give two examples.

steps.title: Check your answers

Examples: folic acid in flour, vitamins A and D in margarine, calcium in plant-based milks, iron in breakfast cereals (any two).

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always distinguish clearly between primary and secondary processing with specific examples. When discussing additives, categorise them by function (preservatives, colourants, etc.) and give examples. For GM food, present both the potential benefits (nutrition, yield) and concerns (health, environment, ethics). Learn the definition of fortification and be able to give at least two real examples used in the UK.
